lead: A DApp is a web page or mobile app that talks to a contract on Ethereum. The page cannot reach the chain by itself: a Web3 library turns a JavaScript function call into a JSON-RPC request, a wallet adds the signature, and a node runs the result on the EVM. Deployment follows the same path with one extra step — a transaction whose data is the contract's bytecode, which the network stores at a fresh address. Teams therefore use a development framework to compile, test and deploy the contract, and then to wire its address and ABI into the front end.
prereq: You need: 5.2 for transactions and gas, 5.5 for Solidity functions, and 5.6 for local chains and testnets.

blocks.text: An Ethereum node exposes its functions over JSON-RPC. Every request is a small JSON object with four fields: jsonrpc (the protocol version, normally "2.0"), method (the function to run), params (an array of arguments) and id (a tag echoed back in the reply). To read a balance the client sends method eth_getBalance with the address and the block tag "latest". Plain HTTP suits one-off requests. WebSocket suits subscriptions, where the node pushes new blocks and event logs to the client as they appear.

A Web3 library writes and parses these messages so the programmer never handles raw JSON. Web3.js and ethers.js are the two JavaScript libraries in wide use. Both take a contract object, encode the call, send it to the node and decode the reply into ordinary JavaScript values. Python and Java have similar libraries.

Two objects do the work. A provider knows a node's URL and transports requests; it is read-only. A signer holds a private key and can produce a signed transaction. ethers.js keeps them separate on purpose, so that code which only reads state can run with no key at all.

In a browser the signer is usually a wallet extension such as MetaMask, which injects a provider object at window.ethereum. The page asks the wallet to sign; the key never leaves the wallet. This is why a private key pasted into front-end JavaScript is a serious bug — anyone who opens the page can read it.

sections.h3: ABI, bytecode and the deployment transaction

blocks.text: The Solidity compiler emits two things a DApp needs. Bytecode is the hexadecimal EVM code that lives on chain. The ABI (Application Binary Interface) is a JSON list describing each public function: its name, argument types, return types, and whether it is view, pure or payable. The ABI is a calling convention, not code. It plays the role a function prototype plays in C — it tells the caller how to pack arguments and unpack results.

To call a function, the library hashes the signature text, for example transfer(address,uint256), with keccak-256 and keeps the first four bytes. That is the selector. Calldata is the selector, then each argument padded to a 32-byte word. Without the right ABI the library cannot build this calldata, so an address alone is not enough to use a contract.

Deployment is a transaction with an empty to field. The data field holds the bytecode, with any constructor arguments appended. The EVM runs that init code, which returns the runtime code, and the node stores the runtime code at a new address. The address is the last 20 bytes of the keccak-256 hash of the RLP encoding of the deployer's address and its nonce, so each deployment from the same account lands at a different address.

A read uses eth_call: one node runs the function against current state, returns the value at once, needs no signature, and spends no gas. A write is a full transaction: signed, gossiped, mined, and paid for in gas. It returns only a transaction hash, not a value. You read the outcome later from the receipt and its event logs.

A development framework automates the loop of compile, test, deploy. Hardhat is JavaScript and TypeScript based; it starts a local chain inside the same process, gives Solidity a console.log, and loads plugins for testing and verification. Truffle is the older tool: it uses numbered migration scripts and usually pairs with the Ganache local chain. Foundry, written in Rust, is a newer option. All three produce a build artifact per contract that bundles the ABI and bytecode, plus the address after deployment.

items: Write the contract in a .sol file and compile it; the artifact holds ABI and bytecode.
Write tests that deploy to a local chain and assert on return values and events.
Write a deploy script that sends the deployment transaction and records the new address.
Point the front end at the node URL and load the artifact with address and ABI.
The user connects a wallet; reads go through the provider, writes through the wallet's signer.

blocks.text: The front end has three jobs. It shows contract state by calling view functions through a provider. It sends changes by asking the wallet to sign a transaction, then waits for the receipt and updates the screen from pending to confirmed. It listens for contract events so the display stays current without a manual refresh. The figure traces one click through these layers.

figure.caption: One click travels down the stack: the page builds the request, the wallet signs it (the key never leaves the wallet), the node runs the bytecode and returns only a transaction hash. The fee appears later in the receipt: 1,500,000 gas × 20 gwei = 0.03 ETH, so a 5 ETH account is left with 4.97 ETH.

spec.aria: A click goes from the user to the DApp UI, the wallet signs the transaction, the page sends it over JSON-RPC to a node which replies with a transaction hash, the node runs the contract bytecode which returns the runtime code, and the receipt later shows a 0.03 ETH fee.

examples.question: A team deploys a contract with a deployment transaction that uses 1,500,000 gas at a gas price of 20 gwei. The deployer account starts with 5 ETH and the transaction sends 0 ETH of value. Find the deployment fee in ETH and the balance left in the account.
steps: Gas used = 1,500,000 gas. Gas price = 20 gwei.
Convert the price: 1 gwei = 10⁹ wei, so 20 gwei = 20 × 10⁹ = 2 × 10¹⁰ wei per gas.
Fee in wei = gas used × gas price = 1,500,000 × 2 × 10¹⁰ = 3 × 10¹⁶ wei.
Convert to ether: 1 ETH = 10¹⁸ wei, so fee = 3 × 10¹⁶ ÷ 10¹⁸ = 0.03 ETH.
The transaction sends 0 ETH of value, so only the fee leaves the account: balance = 5 − 0.03 = 4.97 ETH.
examples.answer: The deployment fee is 0.03 ETH, and the deployer is left with 4.97 ETH.
examples.check:
gas = 1500000
price_gwei = 20
fee_gwei = gas * price_gwei
fee_eth = fee_gwei / 1e9
print(fee_gwei)
print(fee_eth)
print(5 - fee_eth)

examples.question: A read call to a view function is made with eth_call and costs nothing. A second operation writes to storage using 45,000 gas at 40 gwei. What does the write cost in ETH, and what does the caller receive back from the node immediately?
steps: Convert: 1,800,000 gwei ÷ 10⁹ gwei per ETH = 0.0018 ETH.
A write is a transaction, so the node returns a transaction hash at once, not the function's return value.
The return value and events appear only in the receipt after the transaction is mined.
examples.answer: The write costs 0.0018 ETH, and the caller immediately receives only a transaction hash.
examples.check:
gas = 45000
price_gwei = 40
fee_gwei = gas * price_gwei
print(fee_gwei)
print(fee_gwei / 1e9)

traps: An address alone cannot be called. You need the address and the matching ABI; the wrong ABI builds wrong calldata and the call fails or returns garbage.
eth_call is not a transaction. It changes nothing, spends no gas, needs no signature, and returns the value directly. A state-changing send returns a hash and must be waited on.
The ABI is not the bytecode and gives no security. It is only a description of the interface; anyone can write an ABI for any address.
The deployment address depends on the deployer address and its nonce, not on the bytecode alone, so the same bytecode deployed twice gives two different addresses.
Unit slip: gas price is quoted in gwei (10⁹ wei) but balances are in ether (10¹⁸ wei). Multiply gas by the price in wei first, then divide by 10¹⁸.

quiz.q: What is JSON-RPC and which four fields does a request carry?
quiz.a: It is the text protocol a node uses to expose its functions. A request carries jsonrpc (version), method (function name), params (argument array) and id (reply tag).

quiz.q: Name the two compiler outputs a DApp needs from a contract.
quiz.a: The bytecode that is deployed on chain, and the ABI that describes each public function so the library can encode calls and decode results.

quiz.q: Why do modern libraries separate the provider from the signer?
quiz.a: Reading state needs only a node URL and no key. Keeping signing in a separate object lets read-only code run without any private key, and lets a browser hand signing to a wallet so the key never enters the page.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between eth_call and sending a transaction.
quiz.a: eth_call runs one node against current state, needs no signature, spends no gas, and returns the function's value at once. A transaction is signed, propagated, mined, costs gas, changes state, and returns only a hash; the result is read from the receipt and logs.

quiz.q: A contract call uses 900,000 gas at 30 gwei. Find the fee in ETH.
A deployment uses 2,200,000 gas at 25 gwei from an account holding 3 ETH, sending 0 value. Find the fee and the remaining balance.
A front end has the correct contract address but every call reverts or returns empty data. Give two likely causes and one check for each.
quiz.a: First, the ABI may be stale or from another contract, so the selector and argument encoding are wrong; compare the selector with the one computed from the source. Second, the front end may be pointed at a different network than the one holding the contract; compare the chain id reported by the wallet with the deploy network.

quiz.q: Why is a private key written into front-end JavaScript unrecoverable as a security failure, and what should replace it?
quiz.a: All browser JavaScript is delivered to the user, so the key is public the moment the page loads and anyone can drain the account. The fix is a wallet-held signer, where the page requests a signature and the key stays inside the wallet.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the wallet-plus-provider pattern now has a formal name, account abstraction, where a contract account validates its own transactions and can pay gas through a sponsor. Libraries have moved on too: viem and wagmi wrap ethers-style calls for React front ends, and Foundry has become common for Solidity testing in Rust-style tooling. Indexing layers such as The Graph store event logs so a DApp can query history without scanning every block. Search terms to follow: ERC-4337, account abstraction, viem, wagmi, Foundry, contract verification on block explorers, and JSON-RPC method reference.
